1.3 — Your First Script: Variables & Update

Today you write your first C#. This is the lesson where everything else in the year starts, so we are going to go slowly: you will build one small script, and every single line of it gets explained before you type the next one. Nobody is expected to guess anything today.

Reading this on your own? This lesson covers the ground your teacher demonstrated live in class. Work through it in order and you will end up in exactly the same place as everyone else. The script you build here (PlayerLogger.cs) is a throwaway diagnostic tool, not part of the game. Its job is to teach you how a script attaches to a GameObject, what Start() and Update() actually do, and how to make the Console tell you what your code is thinking — three things you will rely on for the rest of the year.
In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I print text to the console?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

Get a script of my own printing to the Console — "how do I print text to the console?" — and keep printing once a second instead of sixty times, so the Console is still readable a minute later.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Make the file something Unity will runOne class in the file, the class name matching the filename exactly, inheriting MonoBehaviour so Unity can attach it to a GameObject as a component. A file that gets this wrong never runs at all.Read: the class Boss : MonoBehaviour row in the quick reference, and the component list you read in 1.2.
  2. Put the two values that have to be remembered in the class bodyA reportDelay tuning knob and a nextReportTime deadline, both declared outside every method. This is the placement decision the lesson turns on: here they are created once and survive the frame, while the same lines inside Update() would be rebuilt and thrown away sixty times a second.Read: the declare-vs-assign split in the One Rule section below, and the [SerializeField] private float speed; row in the quick reference.
  3. Give the deadline its first value in Start()Start() runs once, before the first frame. It sets nextReportTime to the current game time plus the delay, and prints one line so you know the script attached and ran.Read: the void Start() and Time.time rows in the quick reference.
  4. Gate the print in Update() and re-arm the deadlineUpdate() runs every frame, which is far too often to print. The if asks whether the deadline has passed; if it has, print, then push the deadline one second into the future so the gate closes again.Read: the void Update(), Debug.Log and Time.time rows in the quick reference.

Four parts, and only the last one does anything you can see. The first three exist because of one question — does anything next frame need to know about this? — asked three times: yes for the deadline, no for the message, and once for the class itself. Nearly every script you write this year splits the same way: a thing Unity will run, the state it has to remember, the setup, and the every-frame work.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Print to the Console" cannot be looked up. Debug.Log can, and so can Time.time.

Your turn

Four parts, and only the last one does anything you can see. Which of the four would you have written first if nobody had shown you the split — and what would have gone wrong?

Read the Docs ~12 min

Every script in Unity that attaches to a GameObject inherits from MonoBehaviour. That base class is what connects your code to the engine's game loop. These are the five pieces of it you need today — keep this table open while you build:

Engine APISignature / TypeDescription & Behavior
Start() void Start() Lifecycle hook. Called automatically by Unity exactly once, before the first frame. Used for setup and for giving your fields their starting values.
Update() void Update() Lifecycle hook. Called automatically every single frame. At 60 FPS this runs 60 times per second. Used for polling input, checking timers, and continuous logic.
Debug.Log() void Debug.Log(object message) Prints a value to the Unity Console window. Developer feedback — the only way to see what your code is doing while it runs.
Time.time float (read-only) Total elapsed seconds since the game entered Play mode. Constantly increases while the game runs; resets when you stop.
[SerializeField] Attribute: [SerializeField] private float speed; Tells Unity to show a private field as an editable control in the Inspector, without exposing it to other scripts.

Socratic: Lifecycle and Timing

  1. If your computer runs the game at 120 FPS, how many times will Update() execute in a single second? What if it runs on a battery-saving laptop at 30 FPS?
  2. If you write Debug.Log("hello") directly inside Update() with no check around it, what happens to your Unity Console in 5 seconds?
  3. Why does software engineering encourage [SerializeField] private rather than making every field public? (Hint: who should be allowed to change a component's internal variables?)
The One Rule ~15 min

Before you write any code today, read this section twice. Almost every confusing bug you will hit in the next two weeks comes from one misunderstanding, and it is not about Unity at all — it is about where you declare a variable. Get this right and the rest of the unit is straightforward.

The rule: a variable declared inside a method is born when the method starts and destroyed when the method ends. It cannot remember anything between calls. A variable declared in the class body — outside every method — belongs to the object: it is created once and lives as long as the object does.

Why this bites so hard: Update() runs about 60 times every second. So a variable declared inside Update() is created 60 times a second, and each copy starts from scratch and is thrown away. Watch what that does to a counter:

Declared inside the method — broken 
void Update()
{
    int framesSeen = 0;
    framesSeen = framesSeen + 1;
    Debug.Log(framesSeen);
}

Prints 1, 1, 1, 1… forever. The 0 is re-applied every frame, so the counter is reborn at zero before it ever gets to add anything. It has no memory.

Declared in the class body — works 
private int framesSeen = 0;

void Update()
{
    framesSeen = framesSeen + 1;
    Debug.Log(framesSeen);
}

Prints 1, 2, 3, 4… The field belongs to the object, so it survives from one frame to the next and actually accumulates.

Now the part that catches everyone. Look closely at this line: 

float steeringIntent = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");

That single line is doing two separate jobs at once. Reading it as one action is where people go wrong. Pull the two jobs apart:

  • Declaring — float steeringIntent — creates the variable and says it holds a decimal number.
  • Assigning — = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") — gives it a value.

Writing them on one line is legal, and it is perfectly fine when you only need the value for the next line or two. But when you need a value to still be there on the next frame — the direction the player is holding, how much health is left, how many coins you have collected — you must split the two jobs and put them in different places: 

private float steeringIntent;              // DECLARE: in the class body, created once

void Update()
{
    steeringIntent = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");   // ASSIGN: in Update, refreshed each frame
}

Same two jobs, deliberately separated. The variable now exists on the object, so it survives between frames, and Update() simply gives it a fresh value 60 times a second. This split is the shape you will use for every piece of state in this game. You will meet it again in 1.4, where getting it wrong is the difference between a character that moves and one that twitches.

A rule of thumb you can carry. If you want a value to be read and used right now, declaring it inside the method is fine. If you want it to be remembered, it goes in the class body. Ask "does anything next frame need to know about this?" — the answer tells you where the line belongs.

Check the Rule Landed

  1. A student wants to count how many coins the player has collected. Should coinCount be declared in the class body or inside OnTriggerEnter? Say why, in terms of what happens on the next frame.
  2. In the broken counter above, the code reads framesSeen = framesSeen + 1; and still prints 1. How would you explain that result to someone who has not read this page?
  3. Why is it not a bug to declare a variable inside Update() when you use it immediately on the very next line and then never again?
  4. Look back at the [SerializeField] private float speed; row in the table above. Now that you know the rule, why does that line have to live in the class body?
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I print text to the console?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerLogger.cs. By the end you will have a script that prints to the Console once per second — and you will be able to explain every line of it.

Step 1Start the file and name the class

A C# file holds one class. The name of the class and the name of the file have to match exactly — Unity uses the filename to find your class.

using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerLogger : MonoBehaviour
{
  1. 1Tells C# where to find everything Unity provides — MonoBehaviour, Debug, Time. Without it, none of those names exist.
  2. 3Declares a class called PlayerLogger. The : MonoBehaviour part is what makes it a component — a script Unity can attach to a GameObject.The name after class must match the filename exactly, capitals included. PlayerLogger in PlayerLogger.cs works; playerLogger in PlayerLogger.cs throws an error the moment you press Play.

Step 2Put the tuning knobs in the class body

These two lines sit inside the class braces but outside any method. That placement is the whole point of this step — see "The One Rule" above.

    [SerializeField] private float reportDelay = 1.0f;
    private float nextReportTime;
  1. 1How many seconds between reports. The [SerializeField] tag makes a private field editable in the Inspector; the f suffix tells C# this is a float (a decimal number) and not a double.It lives in the class body so it is created once, when the Player is created, and keeps its value for the whole game. If you moved this line into Update(), it would be rebuilt 60 times a second and any change you made to it would be thrown away instantly.
  2. 2When the next report is allowed to happen. private means no other script may touch it — this is PlayerLogger's own bookkeeping.Notice it has no value yet. A field does not have to be given a value at the moment you declare it. Start() will give it one.

Step 3Write Start() — the once-only setup

Start() is a lifecycle method. Unity calls it for you, exactly once, before the first frame.


    void Start()
    {
        nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay;
        Debug.Log("PlayerLogger is alive.");
    }
  1. 2The method Unity runs once when the object appears. void means it hands nothing back when it finishes.
  2. 4Sets the deadline for the first report: the current game time, plus one second. Time.time is how many seconds have passed since you pressed Play.This is an assignment, not a declaration. nextReportTime was already declared up in the class body — here we are only giving it a value. Compare this with the line in the next step that declares *and* assigns at once.
  3. 5Prints one line to the Unity Console so you know the script attached and ran.

Step 4Write Update() — the every-frame gate

Update() runs once per frame — roughly 60 times a second. That is far too often to print anything, so the if is what keeps the Console readable.


    void Update()
    {
        if (Time.time >= nextReportTime)
        {
            Debug.Log("Player has been running for " + Time.time + " seconds.");
            nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay;
        }
    }
  1. 2The method Unity runs every single frame, automatically.
  2. 4The gate. "Has enough time passed that it is legal to report again?" The >= means *at or past*, and the == you might expect would be wrong — frames are not exact.Without this check, the Debug.Log below would fire ~60 times per second and bury your Console.
  3. 6Prints the message. The + glues the text and the number into one string.
  4. 7Moves the deadline one second into the future, so the gate above closes again.Delete this line and the Console floods: the gate would still be open on the next frame, so it would print on every single frame from then on. This is the most common bug in the whole lesson.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

This is the finished file. Do not paste it in — compare it against what you built. If a line differs from yours, you should now be able to say exactly what yours would do differently.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerLogger.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerLogger : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float reportDelay = 1.0f;

    private float nextReportTime;

    void Start()
    {
        nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay;
        Debug.Log("PlayerLogger is alive.");
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Time.time >= nextReportTime)
        {
            Debug.Log("Player has been running for " + Time.time + " seconds.");
            nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay;
        }
    }
}
Bug Hunt ~20 min

You now have a working logger. This section is where you prove to yourself that you understand why it works — by breaking it on purpose, one piece at a time, and predicting what happens before you press Play.

Bug Hunt: Break the Logger on Purpose

Predict the result first, then try it, then fix it:

  1. Move the line nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay; from the class body into the top of Update(), deleting the field. What does the Console do now? Connect this back to the counter example above.
  2. Rename the class to playerLogger (lowercase p) while leaving the file named PlayerLogger.cs. What error appears when you press Play?
  3. Attach the script to the Turret instead of the Player. Does it still run? What does that prove about the relationship between components and GameObjects?
  4. Comment out nextReportTime = Time.time + reportDelay; inside the if. What happens to the Console within 2 seconds, and why does the gate never close again?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Create a new C# script and attach it to a GameObject as a component
  • Explain what runs when: Start() once vs Update() every frame
  • Explain, without looking, why a variable declared inside Update() cannot remember anything — and where it should go instead
  • Split a declaration from an assignment, and say why you sometimes must
  • Write a [SerializeField] private field and explain how it differs from a public field
  • State the rule that a C# class name must match its filename exactly
  • Use Time.time to run something on an interval instead of every frame
